title: The Hungry Choir
premise: Elodie Blackwood, a meticulous property surveyor, is hired to appraise Blackwood House—a decaying estate that shares her surname and seems to appraise her back. As she documents its anomalies, every mirror begins reflecting the room one second late, revealing that the house's previous owners conducted a ritual that 'invited in' a hungry collective consciousness: the Choir, made of everyone the house has ever swallowed. Elodie discovers her own family was among the founders, and that her arrival was not an accident but a summons. To survive until sunrise, she must choose between erasing herself entirely or offering the Choir the justice it was denied—naming, on the record, the crime that created it. She survives by turning her documentation into testimony, freeing the Choir and burning the house's claim on her name, though the last mirror still lags, one second, forever.
about_author: Lena Joubert is a former building inspector from coastal Maine who spent a decade cataloguing condemned properties before turning to horror. She writes about the ways houses remember what their owners want forgotten.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Elodie accepts an appraisal job at Blackwood House despite its uncanny resemblance to her family name. Her POV establishes her compulsive documentation habits and her loneliness. Beat: uneasy curiosity masked as professionalism.

chapters.title: Inventory of Rooms
chapters.summary: Elodie surveys the ground floor, noting impossible measurements—a hallway longer inside than out. She photographs everything; the photos develop slightly wrong. Beat: the first crack in her rational worldview.

chapters.title: The Previous Owner's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the study she finds a ledger kept in handwriting identical to her own, cataloguing the house's 'residents' across two centuries. Beat: recognition turning to dread.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Evening. Elodie notices a mirror reflecting her movements a beat behind. She tests it with a dropped pen. The reflection drops it first. Beat: terror breaking through control.

chapters.title: Documentation as Prayer
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter: young Elodie learning from her mother that writing things down keeps them true. Her POV grounds the theme. Beat: tenderness laced with inherited fear.

chapters.title: The Locked West Wing
chapters.summary: Elodie finds the west wing sealed from the inside. Through the keyhole, a room that is warm, breathing, occupied. Beat: the house becomes a body.

chapters.title: Voices in the Plaster
chapters.summary: She hears layered humming through the walls—many voices, one melody. She records it; the recording plays back her own voice underneath. Beat: violation of the self.

chapters.title: The Neighbor's Warning
chapters.summary: POV shift to Marcus Hale, an elderly neighbor who survived a night in the house in 1974. He begs her to leave before dark and gives her a salt-filled mason jar. Beat: grim testimony, first ally.

chapters.title: Sunset Clause
chapters.summary: Elodie's car won't start; the driveway has grown longer. She accepts she's staying the night. She barricades the kitchen and starts a written log addressed to whoever finds it. Beat: resolve hardening into ritual.

chapters.title: First Verse
chapters.summary: 9 PM. The mirrors show the kitchen as it looked in 1893, with people seated at a table, singing. One of them looks directly out at Elodie. Beat: the dead are aware of her.

chapters.title: The Founder's Portrait
chapters.summary: Elodie matches a portrait in the hall to her own face—her great-great-grandmother, Abigail Blackwood. The ledger lists Abigail as 'First Voice.' Beat: bloodline horror, personal stakes ignite.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Elodie finds the original invitation document: the founders summoned something to 'hold the family together forever.' It interpreted the request literally. Beat: the crime revealed in outline.

chapters.title: Marcus at the Window
chapters.summary: Marcus arrives to help, but the house shows Elodie a mirror-Marcus first—slightly wrong, humming. She nearly lets the wrong one in. Beat: trust under siege.

chapters.title: The Real Marcus
chapters.summary: The true Marcus tells her about 1974: he entered on a dare, heard his dead sister in the walls, and only escaped by refusing to answer. His guilt and grief humanize the danger. Beat: sorrow as survival manual.

chapters.title: Midnight: The Lag Widens
chapters.summary: The mirrors now lag three seconds. Elodie watches her reflection smile before she does. She stops looking at them; she writes instead. Beat: documentation as lifeline.

chapters.title: The Choir's Offer
chapters.summary: The house speaks through the radio: join us, be held, never be alone again. It plays her mother's voice. Elodie nearly answers. Beat: temptation weaponizing her loneliness.

chapters.title: Abigail's Confession
chapters.summary: Hidden behind the portrait, Elodie finds Abigail's true final pages: she tried to undo the invitation and was 'collected' for it. The Choir isn't the monster—the founders are. Beat: the horror reframed as injustice.

chapters.title: The Collected
chapters.summary: Elodie explores the west wing at last; inside are the 'residents,' preserved mid-song, aware, waiting. Among them, a woman with her mother's hands. Beat: grief made architectural.

chapters.title: 1 AM: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: The house appraises Elodie in return—her memories surface in the mirrors, her shames, her small cruelties. It finds her 'undervalued' and offers to 'restore' her. Beat: identity under liquidation.

chapters.title: Marcus's Sacrifice
chapters.summary: The house takes Marcus to the threshold of the west wing, offering him his sister's voice. He almost goes. Elodie pulls him back by singing the ledger's names aloud—naming them breaks the lure. Beat: first victory through testimony.

chapters.title: The Rule of Names
chapters.summary: Elodie realizes the mechanism: the Choir can hold what is unnamed, but named things belong to themselves. The founders kept the victims anonymous in the ledger. She begins restoring names. Beat: the plan forms—justice through record.

chapters.title: 2 AM: The House Fights Back
chapters.summary: The house retaliates: doors relocate, the log pages blank themselves, her handwriting appears in the ledger signing herself over. Elodie rewrites every page from memory. Beat: attrition and defiance.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV shift to Abigail, 1894, in an interlude: her final night, her attempt to name the collected, her collection. Beat: tragic mirror of Elodie's mission, raising the stakes—she failed.

chapters.title: The Founder's Descendants
chapters.summary: Elodie deciphers the ledger's coded page: five founding families, some lines still living. Her own line was meant to 'feed' the house every third generation. She is the harvest. Beat: destiny as predation.

chapters.title: 3 AM: The Hungry Hour
chapters.summary: The Choir, starved of a new voice for sixty years, presses in. The walls sing with her mother's voice, her own childhood voice. Marcus holds the salt line while Elodie keeps writing names. Beat: the darkest hour, endurance as resistance.

chapters.title: The Unnamed Child
chapters.summary: Elodie finds one resident the ledger never recorded at all—a child, erased so completely even the Choir cannot hold her properly. Her lag in the mirrors is the longest. Beat: compassion as the key to the whole mystery.

chapters.title: Naming the Child
chapters.summary: Through fragments—embroidery, a locket, a baptism record sewn into a curtain—Elodie reconstructs the child's name and speaks it aloud. The child's reflection steps forward, whole, and looks at Elodie with gratitude. Beat: the thesis proven—naming frees.

chapters.title: The Choir Listens
chapters.summary: The hungry hum changes key. The residents stop singing the founders' hymn and begin repeating the names Elodie reads. The house shudders; its claim weakens. Beat: hope, and the house's desperation.

chapters.title: 4 AM: The Bargain Refused
chapters.summary: The house offers Elodie everything—her mother alive in the mirrors, her family line restored—in exchange for one unnamed soul to replace the freed child. Elodie refuses on the record. Beat: moral climax of principle.

chapters.title: The Founders' Return
chapters.summary: The five founders manifest, furious, their reflections crisp and never lagging—they were never collected; they are the house. They move to erase Elodie's log. Beat: the true antagonists revealed.

chapters.title: Reading Into Evidence
chapters.summary: Elodie and Marcus barricade in the study and she reads the full testimony aloud—every name, every crime, the invitation's exact wording. Each name spoken weakens a founder. Beat: the trial begins, testimony as weapon.

chapters.title: The Verdict of the Collected
chapters.summary: The residents themselves turn: the named dead face their collectors. The founders' reflections begin, for the first time, to lag. Beat: justice outside any law but truth.

chapters.title: 5 AM: Abigail's Last Page
chapters.summary: Elodie finds the final hidden page of Abigail's confession: the undoing words, never spoken because Abigail was taken mid-sentence. Elodie completes her ancestor's sentence. Beat: generational repair.

chapters.title: Dissolution of the Estate
chapters.summary: The invitation unravels. The west wing exhales. Residents step out of the mirrors as light, then as nothing, each one named as they go. Beat: grief and release braided together.

chapters.title: The Founders' Collection
chapters.summary: The five founders, finally named by their own ledger's last code, are collected by the thing they invited—the Choir takes its collectors. Beat: terrible symmetry, horror's ledger balanced.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: 6:07 AM. The mirrors reflect in real time. The house is only a house—cold, damaged, empty. Elodie appraises it honestly: condemned. Beat: exhaustion, survival, quiet awe.

chapters.title: The Report
chapters.summary: Elodie files her survey with every anomaly documented and every name restored, mailing copies to the descendants of the collected. Justice enters the public record. Beat: purpose found—documentation as testimony, not just prayer.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Epilogue-adjacent: Elodie and Marcus, bound by the night, plant a garden at the house's edge with a stone bearing the child's name. The found family theme resolves in the two survivors and the honored dead. Beat: warmth after horror.

chapters.title: One Second
chapters.summary: Final chapter: weeks later, in Elodie's own apartment, her bathroom mirror lags—one second, no more. She smiles at it, and it smiles back a beat later, almost kindly. She writes it down. Beat: lingering unease, the theme sealed—some things, once documented, remain true forever.
